blocks.title: Aldehydes and ketones
blocks.md:
Both contain the **carbonyl group C=O**. In an **aldehyde** the carbonyl carbon is at the end of a chain (–CHO, suffix **-al**: ethanal CH₃CHO); in a **ketone** it is in the middle (suffix **-one**: propanone CH₃COCH₃). They are made by oxidising alcohols: primary → aldehyde (distil off as formed), secondary → ketone, using acidified K₂Cr₂O₇.

The C=O bond is polar (C δ⁺, O δ⁻); the carbon is attacked by nucleophiles.

blocks.title: Nucleophilic addition and reduction
blocks.md:
**With HCN** (KCN + dilute acid): C=O + HCN → C(OH)CN, a hydroxynitrile; the nucleophile CN⁻ attacks C δ⁺, the intermediate anion then picks up H⁺. The product has **one more carbon** (useful in synthesis).

**Reduction** with NaBH₄ (or LiAlH₄): aldehyde → primary alcohol; ketone → secondary alcohol (H⁻ is the nucleophile). Aldehydes are also **oxidised** easily to carboxylic acids; ketones are not.

blocks.caption: Distinguishing aldehydes from ketones.
blocks.alt: A flow chart: an unknown carbonyl compound gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH; Tollens' reagent then separates an aldehyde (silver mirror) from a ketone (no mirror).

blocks.title: Tests
blocks.md:
- **2,4-DNPH** (2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine): orange/yellow precipitate with any aldehyde or ketone (the melting point of the crystals identifies the compound).
- **Tollens' reagent** (ammoniacal AgNO₃, warm): a **silver mirror** with aldehydes only (Ag⁺ → Ag).
- **Fehling's/Benedict's solution** (warm): blue → brick-red Cu₂O with aliphatic aldehydes only.
- **Iodoform test** (I₂/NaOH): yellow precipitate CHI₃ with CH₃CO– (or CH₃CH(OH)–) compounds.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using 2,4-DNPH to distinguish an aldehyde from a ketone: it detects only C=O in general.
- Forgetting to distil an aldehyde as it forms (it is further oxidised to the acid otherwise).
- Saying that NaBH₄ reduces C=C bonds: it does not (under these conditions).
- Drawing the curly arrow from the C atom instead of from the nucleophile's lone pair.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Deducing a formula
blocks.statement: A compound has 62.1 % C, 10.3 % H and 27.6 % O by mass and M = 58. It forms an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH but no silver mirror with Tollens' reagent. Identify it.
steps: Moles: C 62.1/12 = 5.18; H 10.3/1 = 10.3; O 27.6/16 = 1.73. Ratio ÷ 1.73 = 3 : 6 : 1, so the empirical formula is C₃H₆O (M = 58, the same).
The 2,4-DNPH test shows C=O; no silver mirror means it is not an aldehyde, so it is a ketone.
Propanone, CH₃COCH₃.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Mechanism and yield
blocks.statement: 5.8 g of propanone (M = 58) reacts with HCN to give (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN (M = 85). Describe the first step of the mechanism and find the mass obtained at a 70 % yield.
steps: Step 1: the cyanide ion CN⁻ (nucleophile) attacks the δ⁺ carbon of C=O; the π electrons move to oxygen, giving an anion (alkoxide) intermediate; step 2: this picks up H⁺ (from HCN or acid) to form the hydroxynitrile.
n(propanone) = 5.8/58 = 0.100 mol; theoretical mass = 0.100 × 85 = 8.5 g.
Actual mass = 0.70 × 8.5 = 5.95 g.

blocks.title: Carboxylic acids
blocks.md:
The functional group is **–COOH** (suffix -oic acid). They are **weak acids** (ethanoic acid pK_a ≈ 4.8, K_a ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵) because the carboxylate ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the charge over the two oxygen atoms; they are stronger than alcohols and phenol. Reactions of an acid: with metals (H₂), with alkalis (salt + water), with **carbonates (CO₂ effervescence: the test that distinguishes them from phenols and alcohols)**.

Boiling points are high because of hydrogen bonding (dimers); the lower members are soluble in water.

blocks.title: Esters
blocks.md:
**Esterification**: RCOOH + R′OH ⇌ RCOOR′ + H₂O, catalysed by concentrated H₂SO₄ and heated under reflux (reversible, K_c small). Esters have fruity smells and are used as flavourings, solvents and perfumes.

**Hydrolysis**: with acid (reversible) the ester gives acid + alcohol; with **alkali** (NaOH, heat) it goes to completion giving the **carboxylate salt** + alcohol. The hydrolysis of a fat or oil (a **triglyceride**, an ester of glycerol with three fatty acids) with NaOH is **saponification**, giving glycerol and **soap** (sodium salts of fatty acids).

blocks.caption: Carboxylic acid and its derivatives: reagents for the main conversions.
blocks.alt: A central box for the carboxylic acid with arrows to an acyl chloride, an ester, an amide and a carboxylate salt, each labelled with a reagent.

blocks.title: Acyl chlorides and amides
blocks.md:
**Acyl chlorides** RCOCl (made from RCOOH + SOCl₂ or PCl₅) are far more reactive than the acids: they react at room temperature with water (→ acid + HCl), alcohols (→ ester + HCl), ammonia (→ amide) and amines (→ N-substituted amide): *nucleophilic addition–elimination*. **Amides** RCONH₂ are neutral and are hydrolysed by hot acid or alkali.

Soap from palm oil or palm kernel oil with an alkali is a traditional local product.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Expecting complete conversion in an esterification (it is an equilibrium: use excess of one reagent or remove water).
- Writing the ester as R′COOR: the acid part is the R–CO– part, the alcohol part follows the O.
- Forgetting that alkaline hydrolysis gives a salt, not the free acid.
- Saying acyl chlorides are less reactive than acids.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Ester yield
blocks.statement: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60) is heated with excess ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid to give ethyl ethanoate (M = 88). The yield is 65 %. Find the mass of ester.
steps: n(CH₃COOH) = 6.0/60 = 0.100 mol; theoretical ester = 0.100 mol.
Theoretical mass = 0.100 × 88 = 8.8 g.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Saponification
blocks.statement: What mass of NaOH is needed to saponify 1.00 kg of tristearin, (C₁₇H₃₅COO)₃C₃H₅ (M = 890)? Find also the mass of soap, sodium stearate C₁₇H₃₅COONa (M = 306).
steps: n(tristearin) = 1000/890 = 1.124 mol; each mole needs 3 mol NaOH, so n(NaOH) = 3.37 mol.
Mass of NaOH = 3.37 × 40.0 = 135 g.
Soap formed = 3.37 mol × 306 = 1.03 × 10³ g (about 1.03 kg), plus glycerol.

blocks.title: Structure of benzene
blocks.md: Benzene, C₆H₆, is a **planar hexagon** with bond angles of 120°; each carbon uses three σ bonds, and the remaining p electrons overlap to form a **delocalised π ring** above and below the plane. Evidence: all six C–C bonds have the same length (0.139 nm, between C–C 0.154 and C=C 0.134 nm); benzene does not decolourise bromine water; and the **enthalpy of hydrogenation** is about −208 kJ mol⁻¹, much less than the −360 kJ mol⁻¹ expected for three localised C=C bonds (3 × −120): the difference, **152 kJ mol⁻¹**, is the delocalisation (stabilisation) energy.

blocks.title: Electrophilic substitution
blocks.md:
Benzene's stable ring makes it undergo **substitution** (keeping the ring) rather than addition. The electron-rich π system attacks an **electrophile**.

- **Nitration**: conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄, about 50 °C → nitrobenzene; the electrophile is NO₂⁺ (HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻).
- **Halogenation**: Br₂ with FeBr₃ (or Fe) → bromobenzene.
- **Friedel–Crafts**: RCl or RCOCl with AlCl₃ → alkylbenzene or phenyl ketone.

blocks.caption: Benzene: planar hexagon with a delocalised π ring (shown as a circle).
blocks.alt: A hexagon with an inner circle, labelled with bond length 0.139 nm and 120 degree bond angles.

blocks.title: Mechanism
blocks.md:
1. The π electrons of the ring attack the electrophile E⁺, forming a bond to one carbon: the ring loses aromaticity and becomes a positively charged intermediate (arenium ion).
2. A base (HSO₄⁻ or FeBr₄⁻) removes H⁺ from the carbon bearing E, and the π system is restored; the catalyst is regenerated.

**Phenol** (C₆H₅OH) is more reactive than benzene (the O lone pair feeds into the ring): bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol with no catalyst. Phenol is a weak acid (pK_a about 10): it reacts with NaOH but not with carbonates.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Drawing benzene with alternating single and double bonds as if they were fixed: use the delocalised circle (or Kekulé forms with a note).
- Using bromine water with benzene as a test for unsaturation: no reaction occurs.
- Forgetting the catalyst (FeBr₃, AlCl₃, H₂SO₄) in electrophilic substitution.
- Saying benzene is unreactive: it reacts, but by substitution under harsher conditions.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Delocalisation energy
blocks.statement: ΔH_hydrogenation is −120 kJ mol⁻¹ for cyclohexene and −208 kJ mol⁻¹ for benzene. Use these to estimate the stabilisation of benzene.
steps: If benzene had three separate C=C bonds, the expected value = 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
The observed value is −208 kJ mol⁻¹: less energy released, so benzene is more stable than expected.
Stabilisation = −208 − (−360) = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ (the delocalisation energy).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Nitration yield
blocks.statement: 7.8 g of benzene (M = 78) is nitrated to nitrobenzene (M = 123) with a yield of 75 %. Find the mass of nitrobenzene and name the electrophile.
steps: The electrophile is the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, formed from HNO₃ and H₂SO₄.

blocks.title: Amines
blocks.md:
Amines contain the –NH₂ (primary), –NHR (secondary) or –NR₂ (tertiary) group; they are derived from ammonia. The lone pair on N makes them **bases** and **nucleophiles**: RNH₂ + H⁺ → RNH₃⁺. Alkylamines are **stronger bases** than ammonia (alkyl groups push electrons towards N), while **phenylamine** (aniline) is a much weaker base because the lone pair is delocalised into the ring.

Preparation: halogenoalkane + excess NH₃ (ethanol, heat) → primary amine; reduction of a nitrile (LiAlH₄); phenylamine from nitrobenzene with Sn/conc. HCl, then NaOH.

blocks.title: Amino acids
blocks.md:
An **α-amino acid** is RCH(NH₂)COOH. In solution it exists mainly as a **zwitterion** H₃N⁺CH(R)COO⁻, with no overall charge. It is **amphoteric**: with acid the –COO⁻ is protonated (cation), with alkali the –NH₃⁺ loses H⁺ (anion). At the **isoelectric point (pI)** the net charge is zero; for glycine pI = (pK₁ + pK₂)/2 = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.

In electrophoresis, at pH below the pI the amino acid moves to the cathode, above the pI to the anode.

items.text: two amino acids join with loss of water
proteins: chains of many amino acids

blocks.caption: An amino acid as a zwitterion, and the peptide bond in a dipeptide.
blocks.alt: Text drawings of the zwitterion form of an amino acid and of a dipeptide with the peptide bond boxed.

blocks.title: Peptides and proteins
blocks.md:
Two amino acids join by a **condensation** reaction forming a **peptide (amide) bond** –CO–NH– and water. A chain of many is a polypeptide or **protein**. **Primary** structure: the amino-acid sequence; **secondary**: α-helix or β-sheet held by hydrogen bonds; **tertiary**: folding of the chain by R-group interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges S–S, hydrophobic interactions); **quaternary**: several chains.

Hydrolysis by hot 6 mol dm⁻³ HCl gives the amino acids, which can be separated by **chromatography** (R_f values, visualised with ninhydrin) or electrophoresis.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting to subtract the water when finding the mass of a peptide (M = ΣM(amino acids) − (n − 1) × 18).
- Writing an amino acid as uncharged in water: it is mainly the zwitterion.
- Saying aromatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia.
- Confusing primary and secondary structure: the first is sequence, the second is local shape.

blocks.title: Example 1 — A dipeptide
blocks.statement: Glycine (NH₂CH₂COOH, M = 75) and alanine (NH₂CH(CH₃)COOH, M = 89) form a dipeptide. Find its molar mass and the number of different dipeptides possible from these two amino acids.
steps: Condensation loses one molecule of water (M = 18): M = 75 + 89 − 18 = 146.
Gly–Ala (glycine's –COOH joined to alanine's –NH₂) and Ala–Gly are different compounds.
So two different dipeptides are possible (with the same molar mass 146).
blocks.answer: M = 146; two dipeptides: Gly–Ala and Ala–Gly

blocks.title: Example 2 — Electrophoresis
blocks.statement: For glycine pK₁ = 2.34 (–COOH) and pK₂ = 9.60 (–NH₃⁺). Find the isoelectric point and the direction of movement at pH 2 and pH 11.
steps: At pH 2 (below the pI) the amino acid is mostly the cation H₃N⁺CH₂COOH, which moves to the cathode (−).
At pH 11 (above the pI) it is the anion H₂NCH₂COO⁻, which moves to the anode (+).
blocks.answer: pI = 5.97; cathode at pH 2, anode at pH 11

blocks.title: Addition polymers
blocks.md:
**Addition polymerisation**: unsaturated monomers (alkenes) join with the opening of C=C and **no other product**. Examples: ethene → poly(ethene); propene → poly(propene); chloroethene → PVC; tetrafluoroethene → PTFE. The polymer has a saturated carbon chain with the repeat unit –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ–; it is made of strong C–C bonds and non-polar, so is **not biodegradable**.

Properties depend on chain length, branching and intermolecular forces (low-density and high-density poly(ethene)).

blocks.title: Condensation polymers
blocks.md:
**Condensation polymerisation**: monomers with two functional groups join by forming a link and losing a small molecule (H₂O or HCl).

- **Polyesters** (e.g. Terylene/PET): diol + dicarboxylic acid (or its acyl chloride) → ester links.
- **Polyamides** (nylon-6,6): hexane-1,6-diamine + hexanedioic acid (or hexanedioyl chloride) → amide links –CO–NH–. Proteins are natural polyamides (polypeptides); starch and cellulose are polysaccharides made by condensation of sugars.

Condensation polymers contain polar links and can be **hydrolysed** (partly biodegradable).

blocks.caption: Condensation polymerisation of nylon-6,6 from a diacid and a diamine.
blocks.alt: A scheme showing the diacid and diamine reacting with heat to give a polyamide and water, with the repeat unit mass 226.

blocks.title: Repeat units and degree of polymerisation
blocks.md:
To draw the repeat unit of an **addition** polymer, open the double bond and show the continuing bonds: CH₂=CHCl gives –[CH₂–CHCl]ₙ–. For a **condensation** polymer, remove the ends and join the two monomers' residues: M(repeat unit) = M(diacid) + M(diamine) − 2 × 18.

**Degree of polymerisation** n = M(polymer)/M(repeat unit).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Drawing C=C in the repeat unit of an addition polymer.
- Forgetting the small molecule (H₂O or HCl) in condensation polymerisation.
- Saying all plastics are biodegradable: addition polymers are not, and plastic waste persists in the environment.
- Using the monomer mass for the repeat unit of a condensation polymer (two monomers form one unit).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Nylon-6,6
blocks.statement: Find the molar mass of the repeat unit of nylon-6,6 from hexanedioic acid (M = 146) and hexane-1,6-diamine (M = 116), and the degree of polymerisation for a polymer of M = 22 600.
steps: Each repeat unit uses one diacid and one diamine and loses two water molecules: 146 + 116 − 2 × 18 = 226.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Poly(ethene)
blocks.statement: A sample of poly(ethene) has M = 56 000. Find n and give the repeat unit. Explain why it is not biodegradable.
steps: Repeat unit –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ–, M = 28; n = 56 000/28 = 2000.
The chain contains only non-polar C–C and C–H bonds, which microorganisms and water cannot attack.
So it persists for a very long time as litter; recycling or energy recovery is preferred.
blocks.answer: n = 2000; non-biodegradable due to inert C–C chain
